scenes.narration: This year, Walmart lost a crown it had worn for thirteen years. Amazon passed it as America's biggest company by revenue, by less than four billion dollars. But Walmart still holds another title, and this one isn't close.

In the latest global ranking of family-controlled companies, compiled by EY and the University of St. Gallen, Walmart is number one, with about six hundred and forty-eight billion dollars in revenue. Number two, Volkswagen, had about three hundred and fifty-seven billion dollars. Walmart is almost twice as big.

Here's the strange part. Walmart has been on the stock market for more than half a century, and anyone can buy its shares. Founding families often lose control within a generation or two. So how did the Waltons keep it?
By the end of this video, you'll know Sam Walton's nineteen fifty-three move, how much of Walmart the family's entities hold today, and how much cash flows back to them.

scenes.narration: The story starts on a small-town square. In nineteen fifty, Sam Walton and his wife Helen moved to Bentonville, Arkansas, where Sam opened Walton's five and dime, a variety store selling everyday goods.

Three years later, the business was still tiny, and his oldest child was only nine. But Sam was already thinking about the estate tax, the tax the government takes when a fortune passes to the next generation.

So in nineteen fifty-three, he set up the business as a family partnership. According to his autobiography, as reported by Bloomberg, each of his four children got twenty percent. Sam and Helen kept twenty percent between them. His reasoning, in his own words. The best way to reduce paying estate taxes is to give your assets away before they appreciate.

Let me draw why that works. Here is the gift, made in nineteen fifty-three, when a share of a few variety stores was worth very little. And here is the same stake, decades later, grown into a giant. The arrow between them is all growth, and it happened inside the children's shares, not inside Sam's estate.

scenes.narration: In nineteen sixty-two, Sam opened the first Walmart, in Rogers, Arkansas. And according to Bloomberg, the family's stake stayed inside that partnership structure from then on.

scenes.narration: But a chain of discount stores needs money to grow. And the usual way to raise it puts control at risk.

keyframes.label: A chain needs money to grow…

scenes.narration: In nineteen seventy, Walmart sold shares to the public for the first time, at sixteen dollars and fifty cents each. The money financed a steady expansion. Sam's eldest son, Rob, a lawyer, did what Sam later called most of the work to take us public.

Going public usually means giving up control. But Walmart sold only part of the company, and the Waltons kept their shares together in one family block. Walmart has no special shares with extra votes. Every share gets one vote. The family simply kept enough of them, in one place.

Sam Walton died in nineteen ninety-two, and Rob became chairman. Under Rob, according to Walmart, annual sales grew from about forty-four billion dollars to four hundred and eighty-two billion dollars.
And when Sam died, there was no fire sale of shares to pay a giant tax bill. Most of the stake had been in his children's hands for almost forty years.

scenes.narration: So, more than fifty years after going public, how much does the family still hold?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Today, the family's Walmart shares sit mainly in two places. Walton Enterprises, a family holding company, holds about three billion shares, after a three-for-one split in twenty twenty-four. The Walton Family Holdings Trust held another five hundred and fourteen million in April.

Together, that's about three point five billion shares, or forty-four percent of the whole company, per Walmart's latest proxy statement. At the closing price on November twelfth, by our calculation, they were worth about four hundred and forty billion dollars, in a company valued at about one trillion dollars.
And the trust has given Walton Enterprises an irrevocable proxy, so one entity votes the entire family block, by majority vote of its managing members.

In December twenty twenty-four, the family rewired that machine for the next generation. Rob, Jim and Alice Walton moved their managing roles into four family trusts, and eight younger family members became trustees.

Here's the whole structure. A box for the family trust. A box for Walton Enterprises. An arrow for the proxy, carrying the trust's votes. And Walmart, with one thick arrow of votes going in. Two entities, one voice.

scenes.narration: And forty-four percent is stronger than it sounds, because not everyone votes. At the twenty twenty-six annual meeting, about seven point one six billion shares were represented. By our calculation, the family block was about forty-nine percent of them.

scenes.narration: Control is one thing. But a stake is only worth what the business behind it earns.

keyframes.label: …a stake is worth what the business earns

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: And the business behind it is enormous. In the fiscal year that ended January thirty-first, twenty twenty-six, Walmart had revenue of seven hundred and thirteen billion dollars, ten thousand nine hundred and fifty-five stores and clubs, and about two point one million associates.

But here's the twist. It keeps very little of each dollar. Operating income was twenty-nine point eight billion dollars, about four point two cents of every dollar of sales. That's the everyday low price model. Thin margins, enormous volume.
Thin margins only work with relentless logistics. In the U.S. alone, Walmart runs one hundred and ninety-two distribution facilities, fed by its own private truck fleet and outside carriers.

Let me build sales by business. Walmart U.S., four hundred and eighty-three billion dollars. Walmart International, about one hundred and thirty billion dollars. And Sam's Club in the U.S., about ninety-three billion dollars. The American stores carry the machine.

And on top of the stores, newer businesses are growing much faster. Advertising, sold to brands and marketplace sellers, grew forty-six percent last fiscal year, to nearly six point four billion dollars, including the TV maker VIZIO. In the latest quarter, it grew another thirty-eight percent. Add membership fees from Sam's Club and Walmart Plus, and an online marketplace for outside sellers.

All of that turns into cash. Operations brought in forty-one point six billion dollars last fiscal year. Walmart spent twenty-six point six billion dollars on stores, warehouses and technology, and still had fourteen point nine billion dollars of free cash flow left.

This fiscal year's dividend is ninety-nine cents a share. Multiply that by the roughly three point five billion shares the two family entities hold, and by our calculation, that's about three point five billion dollars a year, about two hundred and ninety million dollars a month, before taxes.
Buybacks help quietly too. Walmart bought back eight point one billion dollars of its own stock last fiscal year, and every share it retires makes the family's slice a little bigger.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: So the machine keeps paying. The real question is whether the family can keep the block together.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Because the block is slowly shrinking. Between December twenty twenty-four and June twenty twenty-six, the holdings trust's filings report sales of about sixty-nine million shares. By our tally of the reported prices, that's roughly seven point one billion dollars. It also handed about thirty-five million shares to family beneficiaries.

The filings say it's to meet the beneficiaries' investment, personal and charitable objectives. The trust went from about six hundred and four million shares to about five hundred million. Walton Enterprises' own block stayed at about three billion shares.

Wealthy families also use trusts the law allows. One is the grantor retained annuity trust, or GRAT. In nineteen ninety-three, Audrey Walton, from the family of Sam's brother Bud, put about two hundred million dollars of Walmart stock into two short GRATs. The IRS challenged her valuation. In two thousand, the U.S. Tax Court sided with her.

Another is the charitable lead trust: it pays a charity for years, then passes what's left to heirs. Bloomberg reported that Alice Walton's mother and brother put more than nine billion dollars into such trusts since two thousand three. And in twenty twenty-six, a trust named a twenty twenty-four Walmart GRAT filed notice to sell shares.

The boardroom has changed too. Rob Walton retired from the board in twenty twenty-four. His son-in-law, Greg Penner, has been chairman since twenty fifteen, and Steuart Walton, Jim's son, is a director. That's two family members out of eleven. And the chief executive since February is John Furner, who started as an hourly associate.

Let me chart the trust. December twenty twenty-four, about six hundred and four million shares. March twenty twenty-six, about five hundred and twenty-one million. June, about five hundred million. The control block is still huge, but it isn't frozen.

And scrutiny isn't going away. At this year's meeting, a shareholder proposal argued that concentrated family control limits other investors' say in board elections. It got about one hundred and twenty-two million votes for, and about six point three nine billion against.

So how did one family keep the world's largest family business? Not with special shares. With timing. Sam Walton gave the company to his children before it was worth much, kept the shares in one block, and let a thin-margin, high-volume machine compound for seventy years. The test now is whether the block holds while pieces of it are sold.
